blocks.text: The lawyer finished reading my husband’s will at 10:42 on a rainy Thursday morning.
Then my stepson, Mark, leaned back in his chair.
His sister, Ashley, immediately asked about the boat.
They had divided almost everything before the meeting was even over.
The investment account was split between the two of them.
Even the antique furniture had been carefully listed.
I sat quietly at the end of the table, listening.
The attorney looked down at the document.
“Approximately ten acres, including the remaining structure of the former mobile home.”
“Your father left that property to Doreen.”
“Don’t feel bad, Doreen. Daddy wanted you to have something.”
“It’s like ten acres of weeds and a burnt-out singlewide. Take it as a compliment.”
Outside, I could hear Mark and Ashley talking in the parking lot.
“Maybe someone will want the scrap metal.”
I stood inside the doorway, holding my purse against my chest.
Because there was something they didn’t know.
Something my husband had never told them.
Something I had kept quiet about for almost a year.
A surveyor had been to that property twice.
And I was the one who had opened the gate for him.
My husband, Daniel, bought the Route 9 property twenty-six years ago.
It sat just outside town, surrounded by farmland and woods.
There was an old mobile home on the property, and Daniel had talked about fixing it up someday.
The Route 9 property became the place where Daniel dumped old equipment, broken furniture, and things he insisted he would “deal with later.”
After he died, I almost forgot about it.
Then, eleven months before the will was read, Daniel’s old friend, Harold, called me.
He asked me to meet him at the property.
When I arrived, another man was waiting beside his truck.
“Your husband asked me to examine the parcel before he died.”
“He contacted me several months before his death.”
Mr. Bell walked the property with me for nearly two hours.
He placed small orange flags into the ground.
He examined an old drainage ditch running along the northern edge.
Finally, he stood near the road and said something that made my heart race.
“Mrs. Carter, do you know what’s happening along Route 9?”
They spent almost the entire afternoon on the property.
When they finished, the surveyor handed me an envelope.
“Your husband told me not to give you this unless the will had been finalized.”
The day after the will reading, I drove to Route 9.
The property looked exactly as my stepchildren had described it.
The blackened remains of the old mobile home.
I walked toward the back of the property.
There, I found the orange survey stakes.
They formed a strange line across the land.
Then I noticed something I hadn’t noticed before.
A new road had been cleared beyond the trees.
The road wasn’t on the property when Daniel and I had last visited.
I pulled out my phone and searched the county’s public planning records.
A major commercial development had been proposed less than two miles away.
And the planned access route ran directly toward Route 9.
The proposed access road needed additional right-of-way.
And my ten acres sat directly beside the proposed connection.
I hadn’t seen it since the week before he died.
“Doreen, if you’re reading this, the children probably think I left you the worst piece of land I owned.”
“That’s exactly what I want them to think.”
The surveyor had discovered that the Route 9 property was strategically positioned beside a planned transportation corridor.
And Daniel had quietly purchased additional rights connected to the parcel.
Because he believed someone would eventually need it.
